title: Two schools
hookLine: the houses of Hillel and Shammai argue, and the Talmud keeps both sides

lines: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT?
cards: Who gets to be right when two serious people disagree? A man comes to a teacher named Shammai with a challenge: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot.

Shammai, the Talmud says, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. He goes to Hillel and asks the same thing. Hillel answers, in paraphrase: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor.
That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it. Two teachers, two temperaments, and around them grew two schools whose arguments fill page after page of the rabbis' writings.

teach.b: In Hebrew they're Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai. A house here means a school: the students, and their students after them.
They disagreed about real things: which blessing comes first on a Friday night, how to light the Hanukkah lamps, whether you must lie down to say the evening Shema.
The house of Shammai often takes the stricter side, but the Mishnah keeps a list of cases where it's the other way. Then the well-known passage, in tractate Eruvin.
The two houses argued for three years, each saying the law follows us.

teach.h: THESE AND THESE ARE THE WORDS OF GOD.
teach.b: Finally a voice from heaven spoke, in paraphrase: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. So why Hillel? The Talmud's answer isn't that they were smarter.
It's that they were gentle and patient.

teach.h: THE LAW FOLLOWS THE GENTLER HOUSE.
teach.b: They taught their own view and the view of the house of Shammai, and even mentioned Shammai's view before their own. The law went to the people who listened best.

teach.h: AN ARGUMENT FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, adds a postscript: an argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. The losing side isn't erased.
Its words are still printed and studied, and some readers say keeping them is a kind of respect: the minority view sits on the page beside the majority, for anyone who comes later.

how: Jewish study often happens in pairs, and the Talmud records minority opinions, including those of the house of Shammai, alongside the law that was followed.

o: the priests and the Levites who served in the Temple
Hillel's and Shammai's houses, who argued and were both kept
the sages of Jerusalem and the sages of the Galilee

games.q: the two schools — tap the pairs.
p: what is hateful to you, don't do
these and these are God's words
an argument for the sake of heaven

s: the law follows Hillel because his school was smarter
the Talmud says it was because they were gentle and taught Shammai's view, even before their own.
the losing side's views were erased from the record
the house of Shammai's views are still printed and studied beside the law.
a voice from heaven called both sides the words of the living God
these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel.

games.q: you're Hillel. a man asks you to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what do you do?
o: give him one line, then tell him to go and learn.
tell him it can't be done.
games.why: Hillel answers: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary. and then: go and learn it.

practice: Choose one person who sees something very differently than you do: faith, politics, how to load a dishwasher.
Try the house of Hillel's habit: say their view to yourself first, as fairly as you can, in words they'd recognize, then say your own, and notice what changes.
You don't have to agree; if you pray, you can hold them in that prayer by name.

wordCard.voice: Two schools. The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, whose arguments the Talmud keeps side by side, and whose law goes to the house that listened.

orig.note: Hebrew: these and these, the start of the heavenly voice's answer in the Talmud.

carryVoice: Your line: the house of hillel. Both sides stay on the page. See you tomorrow.
